A mid mounting fears that artificial intelligence and local-language falsehoods could sway voters in 2027, the Independent National Electoral Commission has rolled out automated verification tools and a multi-agency fact-checking alliance to safeguard Nigeria’s next general elections. The INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Ojo Amupitan, disclosed this on Wednesday in Abuja at a two-day International Multi-Stakeholder Forum on Disinformation in Electoral Contexts in West Africa. The forum, organised by the Fundación para la Internacionalización de las Administraciones Públicas in collaboration with FactCheckAfrica under the European Union Support to ECOWAS in Peace, Security and Governance Project, brought together journalists, fact-checkers, civil society organisations, electoral stakeholders and technology experts from Nigeria, The Gambia and Benin. Represented by his Chief Press Secretary, Dayo Oketola, the INEC chairman said the commission had put verification mechanisms in place to ensure that misinformation did not compromise the legitimacy and credibility of elections. “The commission is working with the National Orientation Agency, civil society organisations, and fact-checking groups to strengthen electoral information management and public confidence amid growing threats from misleading narratives and digitally manipulated content,” he said. Earlier in his speech, the founder of FactCheckAfrica, Abideen Olasupo, described the exploitation of indigenous languages to manipulate public understanding as “hyper-local manipulation,” warning that disinformation actors increasingly target communities underserved by conventional fact-checking interventions. “Strengthening local-language information integrity and improving citizens’ access to credible electoral information are critical to tackling the threat,” he said. He said the forum was convened to examine emerging threats posed by artificial intelligence-generated content, cross-border disinformation, manipulated broadcasts and false narratives spread through indigenous languages ahead of major elections in the region. The Head of Cooperation at the European Union Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Massimo De Luca, said the effects of electoral misinformation could extend to Nigerians in the diaspora, who might also be influenced by misleading narratives about electoral processes and outcomes. He stressed the responsibility of governments and media organisations to work towards curbing the spread of misinformation. The Spanish Ambassador to Nigeria, Félix Costales, underscored the importance of fact-checking in protecting electoral integrity but cautioned against measures that could undermine media freedom and legitimate public discourse. 2027: INEC, NSA read riot act to violence sponsors Communicators urged to embrace AI to boost productivity SAA promotes responsible AI, women’s leadership in technology “The fight against misinformation should not be a weapon against legitimate debates,” Costales said. The Deputy Head of Mission at the Danish Embassy, Julie Rosenkilde Hannibal, reaffirmed Denmark’s support for regional initiatives promoting peace, security and good governance, saying challenges across West Africa required locally driven solutions. Delivering a keynote address, the Director of the International Media and Information Literacy Institute, Dr Sharon Omotoso, called for stronger media and information literacy systems to complement fact-checking efforts. She said misinformation could have particularly damaging consequences for women, who were sometimes targeted with coordinated gendered disinformation aimed at undermining their credibility and discouraging political participation. Omotoso also warned against the politicisation of fact-checking, urging media organisations to maintain editorial independence and exercise caution in verifying names and identifying details to avoid reputational harm. The forum also witnessed the launch of Elect Peace, a digital platform developed by Dataphyte Foundation to connect civil society organisations, fact-checkers, training resources and open-source verification toolkits across West Africa. The platform is expected to strengthen collaboration and improve access to resources for organisations working to counter electoral misinformation. Participants from Nigeria, The Gambia and Benin shared experiences from interventions implemented in their countries, examining the roles of fact-checking, artificial intelligence, media literacy and community engagement in responding to disinformation. Discussions also focused on AI-generated and synthetic media, verification of false information in local languages, technology platform accountability, and the safety of journalists, fact-checkers, women and other civic actors during elections. Working groups subsequently developed recommendations for a Regional Action Plan on Electoral Disinformation, covering civil society and fact-checking networks, media standards, electoral management bodies, regulators, technology platforms, academia and international partners. The proposed action plan is expected to guide regional cooperation and improve responses to cross-border disinformation as countries prepare for upcoming elections, including Nigeria’s 2027 general polls. Dare Akogun
